evidence: Quint. 1.5.47: in participiō per genus et cāsum … peccātur (not checked)
terms.comment: Literally a “fall”, after Greek πτῶσις. The case of a word is asked in the ablative, Quō est cāsū?, and answered Ablātīvō (Traupman 238). The nominative and vocative are the “upright” cases, cāsūs rēctī; the rest are oblique, oblīquī (Varr. LL 8.49; Quint. 1.5.61 rēctō cāsū). Traupman’s Cui cāsuī servit?, what case does it take? (242), uses servīre in a sense not found in Lewis & Short.

phrases.latin: in participiō per genus et cāsum, ut in vocābulō, per tempora, ut in verbō, per numerum, ut in utrōque, peccātur
phrases.english: in the participle one goes wrong in gender and case, as in a noun, in tense, as in a verb, and in number, as in both

phrases.latin: alia cāsūs habent et rēctōs et oblīquōs
phrases.english: some words have both upright and oblique cases
How many cases of nouns are there?
